title: What is an API Gateway, its functions (routing, aggregation, auth, rate limiting, load balancing, caching, logging, fault tolerance), and when to use it?
shortTitle: What an API Gateway is, its functions, and when to use it

s1_definition.profdef: An API Gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of a set of backend microservices and handles cross-cutting concerns on their behalf. Clients send all requests to the gateway, which routes each request to the correct service, and along the way it can authenticate the caller, enforce rate limits, balance load across service instances, aggregate responses from several services, cache results, log and trace the request, and apply fault-tolerance patterns like circuit breakers. It centralizes what would otherwise be duplicated in every service and every client.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the main entrance of National Bank of India. Customers like Rajesh and Priya do not wander into the back offices looking for the loans desk, the accounts desk, and the cards desk on their own. They enter through one front door where a security guard checks their ID, a receptionist directs them to the right department, and a token system limits how many people crowd each counter. The front door does not do the actual banking work, it just controls and directs the flow. The API Gateway is that single, well-guarded front door for all your services.
s1_definition.oneliner: The API Gateway is the single front door that routes, secures, limits, aggregates, caches, and protects, so clients talk to one address and services stop repeating cross-cutting work.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** An API Gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of a set of backend microservices and handles cross-cutting concerns on their behalf. Clients send all requests to the gateway, which routes each request to the correct service, and along the way it can authenticate the caller, enforce rate limits, balance load across service instances, aggregate responses from several services, cache results, log and trace the request, and apply fault-tolerance patterns like circuit breakers. It centralizes what would otherwise be duplicated in every service and every client.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of the main entrance of National Bank of India. Customers like Rajesh and Priya do not wander into the back offices looking for the loans desk, the accounts desk, and the cards desk on their own. They enter through one front door where a security guard checks their ID, a receptionist directs them to the right department, and a token system limits how many people crowd each counter. The front door does not do the actual banking work, it just controls and directs the flow. The API Gateway is that single, well-guarded front door for all your services.

**One line to remember:** The API Gateway is the single front door that routes, secures, limits, aggregates, caches, and protects, so clients talk to one address and services stop repeating cross-cutting work.

sections.s2_technical:
The core function is routing. The gateway maps an incoming path to a backend service. A request to `/api/v1/accounts/**` is forwarded to the account service, and `/api/v1/payments/**` to the payment service. In Spring Cloud Gateway this is expressed as a route with a predicate and a target, for example `.route(r -> r.path("/api/v1/accounts/**").uri("lb://account-service"))` where `lb://` means resolve the instance through the load balancer.

Authentication and authorization are centralized at the gateway so each service does not reimplement token checking. The gateway validates the JWT, confirms the signature and expiry, and forwards a trusted identity context downstream, for example by adding a header after it verifies the token with `jwtDecoder.decode(token)`.

Rate limiting protects services from being overwhelmed. The gateway counts requests per client and rejects excess traffic with HTTP 429. Spring Cloud Gateway offers a `RequestRateLimiter` filter backed by Redis, configured with a replenish rate and a burst capacity, so a single client cannot flood the payment service.

Load balancing spreads traffic across the healthy instances of a service. When the account service runs as three instances, the gateway, using a client-side load balancer, picks one per request so no single instance is overloaded.

Aggregation lets the gateway call several services and combine their responses into one payload, so a dashboard that needs account, card, and payment data gets it in a single client call. With reactive clients this is `Mono.zip(accountMono, cardMono, paymentMono)` which waits for all three and merges them.

Caching stores frequently requested, slowly changing responses so repeated calls are served without hitting the backend, which cuts latency and load. Logging and tracing give one place to record every request and attach a correlation ID so one request can be followed across many services. Fault tolerance wraps downstream calls in circuit breakers, timeouts, and fallbacks, so a slow or dead service fails fast with a graceful response instead of hanging the whole system.

When should you use a gateway? Use it when you have multiple microservices and multiple client types, because it removes duplication of auth, rate limiting, and routing, and it decouples clients from the internal service layout. Use it when you need a single place to enforce security and observability. A senior nuance is to keep the gateway thin: it should handle cross-cutting concerns, never business logic, or it becomes a new monolith and a single point of failure. For very different clients, the Backend-for-Frontend variant runs a tailored gateway per client type.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India exposes three services: an Account Service, a Payment Service, and a Card Service. Today the mobile app knows the address of all three and calls each one directly, and every service has its own copy of the JWT-checking code. When a new service is added, every client must be updated, and when the security team changes the token rules, three services must be edited. This duplication and coupling is exactly what a gateway removes.

Problem 2 — During salary week, one misbehaving client floods the Payment Service with requests and slows it down for everyone, including Rajesh trying to pay rent. There is no central place to throttle a client. This is exactly where gateway rate limiting helps.

The connection to the fix: we will build a small gateway that demonstrates the key functions in plain Java so the mechanics are visible. It will route by path prefix to the correct service, authenticate once by checking a token, rate limit per client with a token bucket, and aggregate account and card data into a single dashboard response.

What the code will do. There is a `GatewayRequest` carrying a path, a client ID, and a token. There is a `BackendService` interface with simulated Account, Payment, and Card services. There is an `ApiGateway` class with a route table, a token validator, a per-client rate limiter, and an aggregate dashboard method. The demo sends several requests: a normal routed call, an unauthenticated call that is rejected, a flood that trips the rate limiter, and a dashboard call that aggregates two services.

```bash
# Real Spring Cloud Gateway run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/api-gateway-service-1.0.0.jar

# Test routing through the gateway
curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer valid-token' http://localhost:8080/api/v1/accounts/SAV2001
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is four kinds of request: a normal account request from Rajesh, an unauthenticated payment request from Priya with a bad token, a flood of seven payment requests from a client called flooder, and a dashboard request for account SAV2001.

Step 1. The account request arrives. The gateway authenticates the token, which is valid, so it continues. It checks the rate limiter for Rajesh, which has tokens available, so it continues. It matches the path prefix to the account service, picks one of three instances through the load balancer, forwards the call, and returns the account JSON.

Step 2. The bad-token payment request arrives. The gateway authenticates and the token is invalid, so it stops immediately and returns 401 without ever touching the payment service. The service is protected from an unauthenticated caller.

Step 3. The flood arrives. The flooder has a token bucket with five tokens. The first five requests each consume a token and pass through. The sixth and seventh find the bucket empty and are rejected with 429. The payment service only ever sees five of the seven requests, so it is shielded from the flood.

Step 4. The dashboard request arrives. The gateway authenticates, then calls the account service and the card service, and merges both results into one JSON payload. The client made one call but received data aggregated from two services.

Step 5. Across all four cases, the services themselves did no authentication, no rate limiting, and no aggregation. The gateway handled every cross-cutting concern, which is exactly the point.

```
  │ + dashboard(id,tok): String  │        │ + tryConsume():bool  │

  1. handle(req)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
An API Gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of a set of microservices and handles cross-cutting concerns on their behalf. Clients send every request to the gateway, and the gateway routes each one to the correct service while taking care of authentication, rate limiting, load balancing, response aggregation, caching, logging and tracing, and fault tolerance. The whole idea is to put the work that every service would otherwise repeat into one place, and to stop clients from needing to know the internal layout of the system.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, the mobile app, the web app, and partner integrations all talk to one gateway address instead of knowing the individual addresses of the account, payment, and card services. The gateway validates the JWT once and forwards a trusted identity downstream, so the services no longer each carry their own copy of the token-checking code. It routes by path, so a call to the accounts path reaches the account service and a call to the payments path reaches the payment service, and it load-balances across the three instances of each service so no single instance is overwhelmed.

Two functions earned their keep immediately. Rate limiting saved us during salary week, when one misbehaving client flooded the payment service. The gateway throttled that client with a token bucket and returned 429 to the excess requests, so the payment service only ever saw a safe rate and Rajesh could still pay his rent. Aggregation simplified the mobile dashboard, which needs account and card data together. Instead of the app making two calls, it makes one, and the gateway calls both services and merges the results into a single payload.

You should reach for a gateway as soon as you have several services and more than one kind of client, because it removes duplicated auth and routing logic and decouples clients from your internal structure. The discipline I always stress is to keep the gateway thin. It should handle routing, security, aggregation, and resilience, but never business rules, because the moment you push domain logic into it, it becomes a new monolith and a single point of failure. A healthy gateway is generic and authoritative about cross-cutting concerns, while the services stay authoritative about the business.
